narrative: The model estimated a 61.7% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than passing, and because your law school application was tied to that risk estimate, admission was denied. That relatively low standing was the top factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your first-year grade decile was the second most important factor; at 3 versus an accepted-student average of 6, it also pushed toward failure, though less strongly. The third most important factor was family income. Being from an upper-middle-income household modestly pushed toward passing; among accepted students, upper-middle income was the most common bracket at 45.4%. It was not enough to offset the two academic indicators. Your LSAT and undergraduate GPA were also below accepted averages, so to improve future chances, focus on strengthening your academic record, consider retaking the LSAT or adding rigorous coursework, and seek admissions advising. You may also ask schools for feedback and apply with a clear explanation of your preparation and improvement plan.
